chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
title: Chick Webb's back and the New York operation
summary: Welburn asks whether Webb's affliction hampered his drumming; McRae recalls his Baltimore fall and the operation he thought hurt him.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

With Chick Webb's affliction, was there any -- did it hamper him in any way playing the drums?

No.
You remember the story on Chick, when he was in Baltimore when he fell down the stairs -- he fell down a flight of steps, you know, and hurt his back.
He probably grew up most of his life with that affliction in his back -- you know, that hump.
They told me --
I was gonna tell you that Chick was telling me at the time when I was talking to him in Baltimore -- the last time I ever talked to him in front of Keyes Restaurant.
I asked him --
I didn't know about it then when we was playing the Paramount Theater -- before we went in the Paramount -- I think they operated on his back.
I remember one of those times he was sick, (Unreadable) we're gonna be off a couple of days

because Chick had to go to the doctor. They had operated on his back.
When we were playing the Paramount Theater, Joe Saunders used to have to take him off the band.
Joe Saunders was -- was the band, there was a valet and was very close to Chick. Like his bodyguard.
Like he used to go around with Chick every place where Chick (inaudible). You know, on the road, or something like that.
Even in New York, he would be there to see that everything was set up -- the bandstand and everything like that.
But he told me in Washinton -- he was going back to John Hopkins Hospital. He said, 'I should've came here first,' because they had all his papers there on him. (Inaudible) when he got hurt.
And they wasn't supposed to do anything -- drain anything out of his back. Whatever they did for him in New York, brought all that illness on him.
